text: processing the worst realization of his evening, and the next the perch he'd been lounging on became a slipway as a high-pressure spray nailed him across the ribs and the cabinet was gone and the wall was somewhere his body was traveling toward at significant speed. The impact drove the air out of him completely, shoulder and cheek connecting with the lockers hard enough to see white, and he had approximately half a second to register that he'd lost the phone before the current got his legs and the floor stopped being a concept he had access to. The knife went somewhere. He didn't see it go. He got a hand on the lockers — fingertips, nothing to grip, the surface slick and featureless — and the current pulled his legs out from under him with casual thoroughness and dragged him out into the hallway proper, away from the walls, into the open water where the pressure waves from half a dozen competing jets were doing something violent to the current. He twisted, trying to get upright, and a wave caught him from behind and flipped him. He twisted again. Got his head above water for a breath, got it driven back under by the next impact. The robes were catastrophic. The long leather danced with the current, becoming a heavy fishing net — wrapping, tangling, adding weight in all the wrong places and drag in every direction. He fought toward the nearest wall, arms pulling hard, and made it approximately a meter before a pressure wave shoved him back into the swirl. Pressure waves knocked him senseless — too strong to fight, too chaotic to predict. His arms flailed wide for something, anything solid, but every grip slipped. He grabbed for a locker door hanging open and got it wrenched out of his hand before his fingers could close. The current spun him, patient and enormous, and pulled him further from anything solid. The mask flooded. It filled all at once, the cowl acting as a funnel, and suddenly there was no air inside it, just cold water pressing against his face from every angle with nowhere for it to go. He choked on the first instinctive inhale, got water instead of air, and his hands found the mask purely on survival reflex — no decision, no thought, just the absolute biological certainty that this had to come off right now. The buckle fought him. His fingers weren't working right, too cold and too clumsy, and for three seconds that lasted considerably longer than three seconds he was just a man underwater in the dark pulling at his own face. Then the clasp gave, the cowl peeled free, and he shoved it away from him. The current took it immediately. No ceremony. Just gone, swallowed into the dark like it had never been there. The water hit his face without it. He'd forgotten what that felt like — the full exposure of it, nothing between him and whatever was coming. He broke the surface gagging, hair plastered flat, water streaming into his eyes. Jets slammed him from both sides, slapping him into debris and wrenching him away again. A floating chair cracked off his shoulder. The tiled floor vanished beneath him; the ceiling overhead lost to the chaos. His robe wrapped around his legs, tangling, dragging. A jet caught him directly across the jaw and snapped his head sideways. He got his arm up too late, took another wave to the ear, and the world tilted hard to the left in a way that had nothing to do with the current. He kicked toward where the wall should have been and connected with debris instead — something solid and angular that spun away on impact and told him nothing about where he was. Another jet found his shoulder and drove him under. He came back up coughing, spitting, the cold of it biting into his face with nothing left to stop it. He couldn't get stable. Every time he found a direction, the competing currents disagreed about it. His hands found the wall. The current tore them free. He found it again — different wall, different section, his palm flat against tile for one lurching second — and then a pressure wave hit from the left and he was spinning again, the robes a dead weight spiraling with him, and the wall was somewhere behind him in the dark. He stopped trying to find it, focusing instead on just trying to stay above the surface. The hallway had no geography anymore. No walls he could hold, no floor he could trust, no direction that stayed consistent long enough to be useful. Just water in every direction and the occasional brutal introduction to something solid that told him nothing except that it was there and then wasn't. He'd been in bad trials. He'd been the thing making them bad, usually — the pressure, the presence, the particular weight of knowing someone was coming and not knowing when. He understood fear from the outside in. Had studied it, cultivated it, learned its specific frequencies and how to play them. He had not, in a very long time, been afraid. The current rolled him and he lost the surface and came up gasping with no idea which way he'd come from, and underneath the kicking and the cold and the roar of water that had swallowed every other sound in the building, something landed that he didn't have the breath or the composure to look at directly. She left me. Not a surprise — he'd understood that the moment he'd checked for his terror radius and found nothing. He'd done the math. He knew what it meant.
